Upset means to disturb something that was in a stable, calm, or ordered state — whether that something is a person's feelings, a physical object, a plan, a stomach, or a competition. Imagine a neat stack of books sitting perfectly on a table. The moment someone bumps into the table and the stack falls, that balance has been destroyed. That is the spirit of every use of "upset" — something that should have stayed in place has been knocked out of its natural, expected position.
Meaning 1: To Cause Emotional Pain or Distress

This is the most common meaning. When something upsets a person, it causes them sadness, hurt, worry, or distress. The person's inner calm — their emotional stability — has been disturbed.

"The harsh comment upset her deeply."
"It upsets me when people are treated unfairly."
"I didn't mean to upset you. I'm sorry."

One thing that makes this word particularly useful is that it is emotionally broad. You don't need to know exactly whether the person feels sad, hurt, angry, or worried. "Upset" covers all of those at once. It simply means their inner peace has been shaken.

In terms of intensity, it sits in the middle. It is stronger than "bother" or "annoy," but not as powerful as "shatter" or "devastate."
Meaning 2: To Physically Knock Something Over or Tip It Out of Position

Here, "upset" describes a physical action — literally overturning or tipping something so it falls or spills.

"He tripped and upset the glass of water on the table."
"The strong waves upset the small fishing boat."

This sense is less common in everyday modern conversation, but you will still find it in writing and literature. It is important to know so the word does not confuse you when you encounter it.
Meaning 3: To Disturb, Disrupt, or Throw Off a Plan, Balance, or System

When something upsets a plan, an arrangement, or a balance of some kind, it throws that plan into disorder. It breaks the expected flow of things. The plan was neatly arranged — and then something came along and knocked it all apart.

"Heavy rainfall upset all of our travel plans."
"The sudden increase in prices upset the balance of the local economy."
"One injury to a key player can upset the whole team's strategy."

Notice how in all these examples, there was an existing order — a plan, a balance, a strategy — and something came along to disturb it.
Meaning 4: To Cause Discomfort in the Stomach

This is a very specific but extremely common use. Certain foods, medicines, or even stressful situations can upset your stomach, meaning they cause physical discomfort, nausea, or pain in your digestive system.

"Spicy food always upsets my stomach."
"The medicine might upset your stomach, so take it with a full meal."
"Anxiety can actually upset the stomach too."

The phrase "upset your stomach" is fixed and very widely used. Whenever you hear it, you know it means digestive discomfort.
Meaning 5: To Defeat a Much Stronger or More Favored Opponent

In the world of sports and competitions, "upset" has a special meaning. When a competitor who was NOT expected to win manages to defeat a much stronger, more favored opponent, we say they upset them. The expected result — the "stable" prediction — has been overturned.

"The young player stunned everyone by upsetting the world number one in the final."
"The small, unknown team upset the defending champions in front of a shocked crowd."

This is also where the noun form "an upset" comes from. If someone says, "There was a major upset in last night's match," they mean the result was a shock — the weaker side won.

"Upset" is an irregular verb, which means it does not follow the normal rules in the past tense. Many learners make the mistake of saying "upsetted" — but that is wrong. All three main forms of the verb are exactly the same word:

Base form → Past tense → Past participle
upset → upset → upset

So:
"This news upsets me." (present)
"That news upset me yesterday." (past — not "upsetted")
"The news has upset me greatly." (past participle with "has")

Also worth noting: "upset" always needs an object. You upset someone or something. You cannot just say "He upsets." You must say "He upsets me" or "He upsets everyone around him."
A Common Idiom: "Upset the Apple Cart"

This phrase means to ruin or disrupt a situation that was running smoothly — especially one that others had worked hard to arrange. Picture a vendor's cart full of neatly arranged apples. The moment someone bumps into it and tips it over, all that careful arrangement is ruined.

"Everyone had agreed on the deal until she upset the apple cart by raising new demands at the last minute."
"Things were going well in the office until his sudden resignation upset the apple cart."
The Thread That Connects Every Meaning

No matter which meaning you are looking at, the same underlying idea is always present: something that was stable, calm, or arranged has been knocked into a state of disorder or discomfort. A person's calm feelings, a glass on a table, a carefully made plan, a stomach's normal functioning, a competition's expected result — in every case, something predictable and settled has been disturbed. Once you hold that single image in your mind, every use of "upset" as a verb will immediately make sense to you.
